candidate.topic: why dopamine fasting backfires for most people
candidate.hook: Trying to "reset" your brain with a dopamine fast is like starving before a buffet—you don't become disciplined, you binge.
candidate.frame: If you've tried a dopamine fast, you know the whiplash. Let's see it through the habit lens: deprivation amplifies craving, cues stay loud, so the rebound is baked in.
candidate.payload: Deprivation cranks up “wanting”: withholding rewards increases the incentive salience of cues, so they hit harder when you re-encounter them (per Berridge & Robinson 2016). Habits are context-tied, and breaking them requires practicing a new response in the same cues; pure avoidance doesn’t update the cue–action memory (per Wood & Rünger 2016; Craske et al. 2014). Result: the fast ends, cues stay loud, and the abstinence-violation effect turns a slip into a binge (per Marlatt & Gordon 1985).
candidate.bridge: It’s crash-dieting for your brain: you starve the craving while the pantry (your cues) stays stocked, so pressure builds. Then the fast ends, and one nibble turns into the whole cake.
candidate.action: Reply with the single cue you’ll retrain this week (e.g., “couch at 9pm”), and I’ll post a 60-second replacement drill in the thread.

Trying to "reset" your brain with a dopamine fast is like starving before a buffet—you don't become disciplined, you binge.

If you've tried a dopamine fast, you know the whiplash. Let's see it through the habit lens: deprivation amplifies craving, cues stay loud, so the rebound is baked in.

Deprivation cranks up “wanting”: withholding rewards increases the incentive salience of cues, so they hit harder when you re-encounter them (per Berridge & Robinson 2016). Habits are context-tied, and breaking them requires practicing a new response in the same cues; pure avoidance doesn’t update the cue–action memory (per Wood & Rünger 2016; Craske et al. 2014). Result: the fast ends, cues stay loud, and the abstinence-violation effect turns a slip into a binge (per Marlatt & Gordon 1985).

It’s crash-dieting for your brain: you starve the craving while the pantry (your cues) stays stocked, so pressure builds. Then the fast ends, and one nibble turns into the whole cake.
